A Dyson Swarm, Made Real
Technical notes
    Technical note

    Taking Mercury apart

    The finished swarm weighs about a sixth as much as Mercury, yet building it takes almost the whole planet, because most of Mercury is iron. The energy to do it is easy to find. What sets the pace is getting rid of the heat that mining leaves behind.

    From docs/full-swarm.md, docs/closed-swarm.md, the manufacturing study and the page’s model · October 2026

    In short

    • Mercury is a ball of iron with a thin rocky skin. The rock, a quarter of the planet, is a quarter silicon and makes 3.4×10²² kg of spacecraft. The iron core has a little silicon in it and makes about 2.5×10²² kg more, at four times the digging.
    • Heat is the speed limit. Every kilogram dug up and thrown into orbit leaves a little heat on the planet, and Mercury can only radiate so much. Paved with radiators glowing at 1,650 K, it can shed 5×10¹⁸ W, which allows about 6×10²⁰ kg of spacecraft a year.
    • Industry doubles every 1.9 years until it hits that limit, from one factory in 2050 to the limit in 2145. After that the swarm grows by a fixed amount a year: half the Sun in 2178, the rock gone in 2200, the Sun enclosed in 2361.
    • Energy is not a problem. Pulling Mercury apart against its own gravity takes about an hour and a quarter of the finished swarm’s output.

    The quarry

    Mercury is the obvious place to start. It is the planet nearest the Sun, so sunlight there is five to eleven times as strong as at Earth and power is plentiful. It has no air, so nothing slows a launch and nothing stands between a radiator and the cold sky. Its gravity is weak: escaping it takes 4.25 km/s, under two fifths of what Earth demands. And it is made of what the film needs: silicon, oxygen, magnesium and iron.

    It is also mostly iron. Its core reaches out to 2,024 km of its 2,440 km radius and holds three quarters of its mass. The rock that the film is mostly made from is a shell only 416 km thick.

    What Mercury lacks shapes the design as much as what it has. It has almost no hydrogen, about 5×10¹³ kg, so there is no water, no organic chemistry and no hydrogen in the solar cells; chip factories must run dry (Hardware after 2095). It has too little potassium for the usual spacecraft coolant, so pods use sulphur dioxide. It has too little iodine, indium or germanium for exotic solar cells, so the cells are silicon. And it has too little silver to coat the mirrors in front of Earth, so they use aluminium, which makes up 5–7% of the crust.

    From rock to spacecraft

    A sail is mostly silicon and glass, and silicon is the element that runs out first. Mercury’s rock is about a quarter silicon. The model assumes that 0.42 kg of finished spacecraft comes from each kilogram of rock (between 0.38 and 0.5 in the other cases), so the crust and mantle can make 3.4×10²² kg of spacecraft. The rest of the rock, mostly oxygen, magnesium, iron and calcium, goes into glass, enamel and structure or is thrown away.

    How far that goes depends above all on how thin the film is. With today’s design, 191 g per square metre, the rock would cover about two fifths of the Sun. The thinner film of the mature era, about half as heavy, covers three quarters of it, crossing orbits included. The last quarter comes from the core.

    Heat is the speed limit

    Every kilogram dug up and thrown off Mercury leaves a little energy behind as heat: the losses of the diggers and crushers, and of the launcher. That heat has to be radiated into space from Mercury’s surface. The surface can only radiate so much, so mining has a top speed. That is the real limit on how fast the swarm can be built.

    Do as little as possible on the planet

    The heat left per kilogram depends on what is done on the surface. The design keeps that to a minimum. Rock is dug, crushed and flung into a low orbit at 3 km/s by an electric catapult, and everything else happens in space, where waste heat can be radiated freely: catapults there add the rest of the speed, and the refineries and chip factories all work in orbit. With superconducting catapults 99% efficient, that leaves about 0.1 megajoules per kilogram on the planet. Every step moved to the surface multiplies it, and divides how fast the swarm can be built.

    How much heat a planet can shed

    Mercury’s bare ground, at about 500 K, would radiate only 2.4×10¹⁷ W. The answer is to pave the planet with radiators and run them much hotter than the heat they carry, using heat pumps, the same machines as in a refrigerator or a home heat pump, driven by power beamed from the swarm. A surface at 1,650 K glows orange and radiates 380 kW per square metre.

    Covering the planet, with corridors between the radiator fields, gives 5×10¹⁸ W of capacity for mining heat. Hotter radiators help less than one might expect: at 2,000 K, about as hot as such materials can run, the figure rises only to about 9×10¹⁸ W. At 1,650 K, sunlight adds only 2.4% to what a radiator must shed, so the fields work by day as well as by night.

    Divide one number by the other: 5×10¹⁸ W of capacity at 0.1 MJ per kilogram is 50 trillion kilograms of rock a second, and 21 trillion kilograms of spacecraft. Some of that goes into replacing worn-out factory machines, which leaves 5.9×10²⁰ kg of sails a year.

    Could the rock carry its heat away with it?

    It is tempting to dump the waste heat into the rock being launched, so that it leaves the planet. It does not work for the catapult, whose superconducting coils must stay cold: the rock would have to be heated through a heat pump, which costs more than it removes. The core is different. It is already molten at 1,800–2,000 K, so it is launched hot, and the heat it holds leaves with it.

    How fast it grows

    The build starts with one factory of a thousand tonnes, landed on Mercury in 2050. A factory that builds copies of itself grows exponentially. Copying everything takes about a year; growing the chip factories as well adds 0.9 years, so the whole industry doubles every 1.9 years (Hardware after 2095).

    From a thousand tonnes to the heat limit’s 6×10²⁰ kg a year is about fifty doublings, 95 years. For most of that time there is almost nothing to see: the first sails fly in the 2050s, but the swarm catches only a millionth of the Sun by 2116. Then the end of the doubling arrives quickly: one in ten thousand in 2129, one per cent in 2141, and the heat limit in 2145.

    After the limit, the swarm grows by a fixed mass each year. Each new year adds the same tonnage, but a smaller share of what is already there.

    Other estimates of how fast Mercury could be dismantled are much quicker. Armstrong and Sandberg (2013) are reported to give about 31 years. That figure reaches us through summaries of their paper rather than its text, and it does not seem to count the heat left on Mercury, which here is what sets the pace.

    The iron core

    Mercury’s core is iron and nickel with some silicon dissolved in it. How much is uncertain: published estimates run from under 1% to 25%, and the model takes 6%, about a quarter of the rock’s share. So every kilogram of spacecraft from the core means digging and lifting four times as much material, and leaving four times the heat behind.

    The core is lifted while still molten and refined in orbit. Its iron is not wasted: it becomes shielding, structure, and mass for the catapults to throw. The closed swarm needs 5.67×10²² kg in all. The crust and mantle provide 3.38×10²² kg and are used up in 2200, with the sphere three quarters closed; every sail after that comes from the core. By 2361, 93% of Mercury, and 91% of its core, has been taken apart.

    Without the core, the swarm would stop at three quarters of the Sun. This is the most uncertain input in the whole model: if the core holds as little as 1% silicon the sphere cannot close from Mercury alone; if it holds 25%, the core could build the whole swarm by itself.

    Repairs, and what comes after

    A finished swarm still uses material. Each sail is rebuilt every 300 years and 1% of it is lost each time, so the closed swarm loses about 1.9×10¹⁸ kg a year. What is left of Mercury after 2361, mostly core, covers that for about 1,200 years. With 99.9% recycling it would last 12,000 years.

    With today’s kind of sails, lasting 15 years and recycled at 94%, the loss would be 2.3×10²⁰ kg a year, more than a hundred times as much. The core’s silicon would go on replacements and the sphere would never close. Long-lived sails are not a refinement: they are what makes enclosing the Sun possible with one planet.

    Asteroids matter more for what Mercury lacks. Ceres alone probably holds about 10²⁰ kg of water, with some 10¹⁹ kg of hydrogen in it, two hundred thousand times what Mercury has.

    Energy is never the limit

    The energy needed to pull Mercury apart against its own gravity is about 1.8×10³⁰ J. The finished swarm collects 3.8×10²⁶ W, so it could pay that in about an hour and a quarter. Making all of its hardware, at about 1,150 MJ per kilogram, takes about two days of its output. Over the centuries the build takes, energy never holds it back. What does is the rate at which heat can leave Mercury, the rate at which chip factories can grow, the amount of silicon in the planet, and how long each sail lasts.

    Open questions

    • How much silicon is in the core. From under 1% to 25% in the literature; it decides whether one planet is enough.
    • Catapult efficiency. 99% instead of 95% triples the speed limit. Superconducting catapults at this scale have never been built.
    • Radiators at 1,650 K covering a planet, made from Mercury’s own heat-proof materials, and lasting centuries.
    • Yield. 0.42 kg of spacecraft per kg of rock assumes most of the silicon reaches the film.
